tasks.query: Context: a laboratory ultrasonic atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder, the 3D Lab ATO type): an induction-melted charge in a graphite crucible drains through a nozzle as a thin stream or as drips onto the tip region of a thin vibrating sonotrode plate at about 40 kHz, under argon. On 2026-10-08 a run with an aluminium 6xxx-series charge at about 850 C, a carbon-fibre-reinforced-carbon (CFC) plate and the 1:1.5 booster mounted reversed (1.5:1, about 67 % of the 1:1 amplitude; the generator amplitude slider was at 92-100 %) gave essentially no powder: the first melt froze into a lump at the plate tip, later melt built up on the plate and dripped off un-atomized into the catch cup. Earlier runs with a molybdenum plate at the same reduced amplitude atomized, and runs with the CFC plate at the amplifying (1:1.5) booster setting atomized. The trainer says aluminium wets CFC by reacting with it, that aluminium wets molybdenum through Mo-Al reactivity, that metal plates are thin and heat up faster, and that at low amplitude atomization is 'slower, more sensitive, more fragile' with a risk of 'no atomization suddenly because the vibrations could be too weak'. Question: from the peer-reviewed literature on ultrasonic atomization of liquid metals (and of liquids generally), explain what determines whether a melt stream delivered to a vibrating plate atomizes versus wets, pools, freezes and drips off, with emphasis on: (1) the vibration amplitude / surface acceleration threshold for capillary-wave (Faraday) atomization and how it scales with frequency, surface tension, density and viscosity; give the standard equations (Lang's droplet-size equation, the critical-amplitude expressions) and evaluate them numerically for liquid aluminium at about 40 kHz (surface tension 0.85-0.9 N/m, density 2.37 g/cm3, viscosity 1.2 mPa s); (2) how reducing the amplitude by a factor of about 1.5 changes the maximum liquid feed rate that can be fully atomized, the droplet size and the atomization efficiency; (3) the role of melt-sonotrode wetting and of the sonotrode material: molten aluminium on carbon/graphite/CFC versus on molybdenum (and titanium), including the alumina skin as a wetting barrier, Al4C3 and Mo-Al intermetallic formation, and how ultrasonic cavitation breaks the oxide film and promotes wetting (ultrasonic-assisted wetting and ultrasonic soldering literature); (4) the sonotrode thermal condition: freezing of the first melt on a cold tip, plate pre-heating, and the thickness and temperature of the liquid film needed for stable atomization; (5) any reported operating amplitudes (micrometres), yields and failure modes for ultrasonic atomization of aluminium or other metals (for example the 3D Lab / AMAZEMET papers by Zrodowski, Wysocki, Kalicki and co-workers, the NASA and Lierke work, Mahdi and co-workers, Lecours and co-workers). Give quantitative values and cite the sources.

Does molten aluminium wet carbon (graphite, vitreous carbon, carbon fibre, carbon-fibre-reinforced carbon)? Summarize sessile-drop contact angle versus temperature and time (for example the transition from non-wetting above 120 degrees to wetting below 90 degrees as Al4C3 forms, and the temperatures and holding times at which it happens), the effect of the aluminium oxide skin and of oxygen partial pressure, the role of alloying elements such as Si and Mg, and whether mechanical or ultrasonic vibration accelerates the wetting. Compare with molten aluminium on molybdenum: contact angle, the intermetallics that form (Al12Mo, Al5Mo, Al8Mo3, Al3Mo), their growth kinetics at 700-900 C and how fast a molybdenum substrate is consumed. Which of the two substrates is wetted faster by liquid aluminium at 700-850 C, and why? Cite the sources with numbers.

In ultrasonic atomization of a liquid film on a vibrating surface (20-60 kHz), what is the minimum vibration amplitude or surface acceleration needed to start droplet ejection, how does that threshold scale with the liquid's surface tension, viscosity and density and with the frequency, and what happens to the liquid below the threshold (standing capillary waves without ejection, film spreading, run-off or dripping)? Include values measured or computed for liquid metals (tin, zinc, aluminium, gallium alloys, solders) and for water as a reference, and the relation between amplitude and atomization throughput: the maximum flow rate that is fully atomized, and the liquid overloading or flooding regime in which excess liquid runs off un-atomized. Give equations and numbers with citations.

Has anyone reported ultrasonic atomization of aluminium or aluminium alloys in which the melt failed to atomize and instead built up, froze or dripped off the sonotrode, and attributed it to insufficient vibration amplitude, a cold sonotrode or poor wetting of a carbon or graphite sonotrode? Has anyone compared carbon (graphite or carbon-fibre-reinforced carbon) versus molybdenum or titanium sonotrode plates for aluminium ultrasonic atomization (3D Lab ATO, AMAZEMET rePowder or research rigs)?
